analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban congressional stock trading never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependents from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, derivatives, and similar investments. Members would have 90 days to sell those holdings or put them into a qualified blind trust. They could still own diversified mutual funds, U.S. Treasury securities, state and local bonds, and their federal retirement plan. Members would have to file a public certificate of compliance, and willful violations could bring a civil penalty of up to $50,000 from the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans gain a rule that members of Congress cannot profit from buying and selling stocks while their own votes and committee work move markets. Honest members also gain, because their public certificates of compliance would be posted online. The penalty cannot be paid with official office funds or campaign money, so violating members would bear it personally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want Congress barred from stock trading

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members, their spouses, and dependents from owning or trading individual securities, security futures, commodities, and derivative bets on them, closing a route by which lawmakers can trade on information from their official work.

Requires divestiture within 90 days, either by sale or by placing the assets in a qualified blind trust whose trustee may not tell the member what the trust holds and must certify annually that no information was shared.
Requires every member to submit a pledge of compliance and makes the resulting certificates publicly available on a government website, so voters can see who is and is not in compliance.

Directs the ethics office to refer willful violators to the Attorney General, who may seek a civil penalty of up to $50,000 that cannot be paid from office allowances or campaign funds; losses from violating trades also cannot be deducted from income taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their households, who would have to sell individual stock holdings within 90 days or hand them to a blind trust, giving up direct control of those investments while in office. Members with large individual portfolios would bear the largest compliance burden.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their households

drawbacks.text: The $50,000 penalty cap is small next to what a large portfolio can gain from a well-timed trade, so the financial deterrent is modest.
Enforcement depends on the supervising ethics office finding reasonable cause and referring members to the Justice Department; the bill creates no independent prosecutor or automatic audit.

Members could still own broad, diversified investment funds, Treasury securities, and state and local bonds, so their household wealth would still rise and fall with the markets they legislate over, just less directly.

An honest objection is that forcing members to divest or use blind trusts could make it harder to recruit candidates with business experience and could push members' finances into arrangements that are less transparent to the public, not more.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is integrity: lawmakers would no longer be able to trade individual companies whose fortunes their own decisions affect, and compliance would be publicly certified. The costs fall almost entirely on the members themselves, which is the point of the bill. The design has real limits, chiefly a small penalty and enforcement that runs through the same ethics machinery members already answer to, but on balance it would meaningfully restrict a conflict of interest that now goes unregulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in April 2023, neither one ever reported it, and no one ever brought it to the floor before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the bill on April 28, 2023 with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Matt Gaetz, and Raja Krishnamoorthi as original cosponsors, pairing a Republican sponsor with Democratic and Republican co-signers.
The bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration and to the Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced.
No further action is recorded: neither committee held a markup or reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans, in addition to its Republican sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress came out ahead: because the bill died without a vote, they keep the current rules, which allow them and their families to own and trade individual stocks while serving, with only existing disclosure requirements standing in the way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was genuinely mixed by party: a Republican sponsor joined by three Republicans and four Democrats, with no recorded opposition vote because no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill would have stripped members, spouses, and dependents of the ability to own and trade individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives while in office. Because the bill died, that ability stays intact under existing disclosure rules, which do not bar trading.
